A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Editing Overfit, EVOKE and LTI research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original GPT-J and GPT-2 XL experiments, mitigation studies, LTI ablations and a generation case study in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds Llama-2-7B evaluation results in Appendix G, Tables 5–6.

M1.justification: Section 6 retains the same subject-representation, output-distribution and new-knowledge constraints, optimization objective and editing procedure. Renaming LTI from Learn to Inference to Learn the Inference does not change the method.

E1.justification: Both versions use COUNTERFACTPLUS and the same six EVOKE tasks, with unchanged source datasets and benchmark composition. Adding Llama-2-7B changes the evaluated model, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The existing comparisons retain FT, FT-L, MEND, ROME and MEMIT. The new Llama-2-7B comparisons reuse FT, FT-L, ROME and MEMIT; newly discussed MeLLo, DecK and StruEdit are not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 adds Llama-2-7B as an evaluated backbone with model-specific settings, extending the existing EVOKE protocol. The GPT-J/GPT-2 XL settings, data construction, sample counts and evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The norm-constraint, batch-editing, data-augmentation, constraint-ablation and layer-sensitivity studies are retained, as is the generation case study. Appendices E–G become H–J; the new Llama tables add model evaluation rather than a new diagnostic analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. V2 continues the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 5–6 add Llama-2-7B results; retained GPT results are unchanged. The new MEMIT/MEMIT-LTI comparison reports multi-hop EOS of 48.18/67.52 and paraphrase AMS of 96.80/91.71, extending the existing mitigation findings and their tradeoffs to another backbone.

T1.justification: The metric definitions in Section 3.1, LTI equations (1)–(5), and ROME mathematical treatment in equations (6)–(9) are unchanged. Moving the ROME appendix from D to F adds no mathematical development.

C1.justification: The abstract replaces the qualified claim that common mitigation strategies have 'limited effectiveness' with the categorical claim that they are 'ineffective.' The central Editing Overfit, EVOKE and LTI contributions otherwise retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: New Appendix A explicitly identifies dependence on accurate in-context learning, possible failure with stubborn prior knowledge, and restricted applicability to structured factual edits. These specific limitations were absent from v1's general future-work discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices D–E add Llama-2-7B implementation information: baseline settings follow Yao et al. (2023), SRC uses layer 15, and the new-knowledge coefficient is 0.35 for ROME-LTI and 0.125 for MEMIT-LTI. Existing GPT implementation details are retained.

R1.justification: New Appendix B explains LTI's relationship to in-context editing, MeLLo, DecK and StruEdit, adding the two Bi et al. references. V2 also adds the Llama 2 reference and removes the introductory SERAC/T-patcher discussion and citations, while retaining its central research positioning.

P1.justification: V2 revises the opening paragraph, renames LTI in key passages, shortens the conclusion, corrects several errors, and adds acknowledgements and appendix sections. Existing appendices are renumbered, and author/header information changes; most prose and the main narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 5–6 and reflows existing appendix tables and figures around the additions. Figures 1–10 and Tables 1–4 retain their substantive display designs, with limited placement, spacing and header changes.

improvement.justification: The Llama-2-7B experiments strengthen evidence that the findings extend beyond the two GPT backbones, while the new limitations and related-work discussion clarify applicability and positioning. These modest gains outweigh the abstract's overgeneralization that common mitigation strategies are ineffective, despite retained evidence that specificity augmentation helps.
